CHIEF COMPLAINT
Back of the heel hurts, typically after a workout or when first getting up in the morning, extending all the way up into the calf.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is training for a triathlon (running about 10 kilometers in the morning, biking 45 minutes to an hour at lunchtime, and swimming 30 minutes to an hour in the evening, 5 days a week; on weekends alternates between a long run and a long bike ride, taking one day off). The patient does not stretch. Pain occurs mainly on the right side. It is present after activity and first thing in the morning when getting out of bed, feeling really tight and almost like it's tearing. It eases up after walking around for 10-15 minutes, but becomes really sore again after sitting for an extended period or after a lot of activity.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Lower extremities examined. Left leg does not hurt; pain is mainly on the right.
- Pulling toes up towards him creates a little bit of pain.
- Pushing foot against doctor's hand hurts a little bit.
- Squeezing left calf: no pain on the left side.
- Squeezing right calf: no pain.
- Thompson test: negative.
- Pressing on right heel: causes significant pain.
- Running up the Achilles tendon: real tender.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Diagnosis: Achilles tendinitis, from overuse due to aggressive triathlon training.
- Plan:
  - Stop training for a week or two to allow healing.
  - Take ibuprofen (Advil) three tablets every six hours as an anti-inflammatory.
  - Physical therapy ordered for strength and stretching education.
  - Follow-up in 7 to 10 days following the first couple of physical therapy appointments to monitor progress.
  - X-ray not indicated at this time, but may consider more aggressive treatment if significant pain continues after 10 days without activity modification.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up of chronic problems (depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Edward is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history of depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair who presents for a follow-up. 
- Depression: Patient is doing well, seeing a counselor once a week, and swimming at the pool. He does not want to start medications at this time.
- Hypertension: Patient takes Norvasc daily and checks his blood pressure at CVS pharmacy about once a week. He admits to occasional burgers and wine. He reports mild swelling in his ankles mainly near the end of the day, which goes away by the next morning.
- Rotator cuff repair: Done about eight months ago. Patient is doing well, stretching with a yoga ball, progressing to home exercises, and getting stronger.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for nasal congestion, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Positive for mild ankle swelling near the end of the day.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Vital signs: Blood pressure elevated at 156/94.
- Heart: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, stable compared to the past.
- Lungs: Clear.
- Extremities: 1 to 2+ pitting edema in the legs.

RESULTS
- Labs: Creatinine and overall lab results look stable and really good.
- EKG: Normal EKG, fine, no evidence of coronary artery disease.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Depression: Doing well with counseling and lifestyle strategies. No medication indicated at this time; patient knows to call if needed.
2. Hypertension: Not well controlled. Increase Norvasc to 10 mg a day. Order an echocardiogram and a lipid panel. Discussed decreasing salt intake regarding ankle edema.
3. Rotator cuff repair: Doing very well, progressed to home exercises. Condition is resolved; no further intervention needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up visit for diabetes management, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female who presents for a follow-up. Her recent A1C was 9.9, indicating poorly controlled blood sugars. She has been taking glimepiride 2 mg, but the plan is to increase it to 4 mg twice a day (taking two 2 mg pills twice a day with current supply, and a new prescription will be written for 4 mg twice a day). She does not eat much pasta, rarely has bread (prefers wheat bread, usually two slices in the morning), and avoids sodas, preferring club soda and seltzer water. She continues to smoke and is not ready to quit. She recently had cataract surgery with Dr. Sanchez at Liberty Road and got new glasses. She reports foot and leg pain/discomfort ("feet feel like hell," pain up to hip), which the doctor identifies as peripheral neuropathy. She also reports a recent cough with clear congestion, but no fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain, or GI symptoms.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Feeling totally normal. No headaches or dizziness.
Eyes: Vision improved with cataract surgery, though she notes one lens feels a bit funny.
Respiratory: Coughing lately due to congestion (clear mucus), improved this morning. No shortness of breath, fever, chills, or wheezing.
Cardiovascular: No chest pains, pressure, or tightness.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or other GI symptoms.
Genitourinary: Slower stream, but stable and urinates several times per day. Gets up at night once in a while.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Carotids: Normal, pulse without bruits.
Heart: Rhythm is regular, normal rate, S1 and S2 are crisp. No murmurs.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation. No rasps or wheezing.
Extremities: Without edema. Pulses are palpable on dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial. Thickened nails, mildly dry skin, no skin breakdown. Mildly decreased sensation in the tips of the first and second toes.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Diabetes mellitus: Poorly controlled (A1C 9.9). Increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice a day (take two 2 mg pills twice a day of current supply; new prescription for 4 mg twice a day). Continue metformin. Watch for signs of low blood sugar (weakness, shakiness, sweating).
2. Peripheral neuropathy: Mildly decreased sensation in toes, foot/leg discomfort. Keep feet moisturized; patient may use a foot scrub/cream.
3. Hypertension: BP rechecked at 140/60. Continue current medication combination (metoprolol 50 mg daily, lisinopril with hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily). Check kidney function with today's lab work.
4. Hypercholesterolemia and vascular disease: Continue high-dose atorvastatin.
5. Tobacco use: Patient continues to smoke; advised on cessation.
6. Labs: Blood work to be drawn today (including kidney function and blood work for sugars).
7. Follow-up: Return in four months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up from emergency room visit for shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Louis is a 58-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure who presents for follow-up after an ER visit. On Saturday, while playing tennis in hot and humid weather, he experienced shortness of breath and difficulty breathing after about half an hour. He thought he was having a heart attack, became very nervous, and his wife took him to the ER. Everything checked out at the ER, but he was very upset about it. About six hours after getting home, he felt very light-headed and dizzy. By Sunday, he felt fine. He reports taking all of his heart failure medications diligently and watching his diet/avoiding salt, though he admits to cheating every now and then. 

In addition, he reports his cataract surgery from three months ago has been fine with no vision problems, and his skin cancer removal from five months ago healed up nicely with no problems.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Denies acute distress, felt light-headed and dizzy about six hours after the ER visit, but felt fine by Sunday. 
Eyes: No vision problems. 
Cardiovascular: Shortness of breath on exertion (playing tennis in the heat). Denies chest pain. 
Respiratory: Shortness of breath while playing tennis. 
All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Very supple, no jugular venous distention.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur. Blood pressure is a little high (noted to be high in the ER as well).
Lungs: Fine crackles bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema in both legs.

RESULTS
ECG: Stable ECG showing left ventricular hypertrophy.
Echocardiogram: Pumping function of the heart is a little low, but stable.
Skin Biopsy / Pathology: Confirms complete removal of skin cancer, margins clear ("they got all of that and everything's fine").
ER Report: Noted high blood pressure.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Short of breath / Congestive heart failure exacerbation: Likely precipitated by heat and dietary indiscretion (eating salty foods leading to fluid retention). 
- Prescribe an extra dose of Lasix 80 mg once a day.
- Prescribe Carvedilol 25 mg twice a day.
2. Blood pressure: Elevated today and in the ER; monitored and managed via heart failure regimen adjustments.
3. Cataract surgery and skin cancer removal: Both healed and stable, no medication adjustments needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lower back injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a male presenting with lower back pain that began approximately 4 months ago while moving boxes during his son's college dorm move-out. He initially felt like he was going to topple over and could not support his upper body weight, along with temporary tingling in the toes of his right foot that resolved after about an hour. He reports occasional leg weakness when carrying heavy items. He experiences sharp lower back pain when turning certain ways or rolling over in bed, which resolves with repositioning. He has tried Tylenol, ibuprofen, heat, and ice with little relief; ibuprofen helps slightly for a shorter duration, with no stomach upset. He previously went to an urgent care where an MRI was recommended, but he declined due to insurance concerns. He denies any bladder or bowel incontinence or retention. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Denies fevers or chills.
Neurological: Denies ongoing numbness or tingling in the feet. Denies leg weakness except when carrying heavy items.
Genitourinary/Gastrointestinal: Denies bladder or bowel incontinence or difficulty going to the bathroom.
All other systems reviewed and negative except as noted in the HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Temperature normal, Blood Pressure 117/56, Heart Rate 68, Oxygen saturation 95% on room air.
Neck: Bony protuberance of C5-C6 noted. No pain to palpation of the neck.
Lumbar Spine: No pain to palpation of the lumbar spine. Decreased flexion and extension of the lower back. Positive straight leg raise. Paraspinal muscle spasm of the lumbar spine noted.
Musculoskeletal: Lower extremities strength is equal bilaterally. Right knee has a well-healed total knee replacement from the spring of 2020 (about 2 years ago), feels about 95%.

RESULTS
Lumbar spine x-ray showed no acute bony abnormality and no fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute disc herniation (symptoms ongoing for a few months).
2. Order lumbar spine MRI to evaluate soft tissues.
3. Refer to physical therapy through the health system.
4. Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg once a day.
5. Discussed potential future treatment options including epidural steroid injection if a herniated disc is confirmed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain after dropping a landscape brick on it.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Elijah is a patient referred by his primary care provider who presents with right foot pain after dropping a landscape brick on his foot yesterday while doing yard work. He was able to keep working initially despite the pain, but the foot subsequently became swollen. He rates his pain as 11 out of 10. He reports numbness in the whole foot, noting it has been that way for a long time. He has not taken any medications for the pain. He reports a past history of breaking his ankle 20 years ago and previous surgery on his other ankle.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals look good. Focused exam of the right foot shows bruising on the bottom and top parts of the foot, associated swelling, and tenderness to palpation for the midfoot. Neurovascular exam of the right foot reveals brisk capillary refill in less than three seconds, a strong bounding dorsalis pedis pulse, and motor and sensation intact, matching bilaterally.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot shows dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal with a 3-millimeter separation of the first and second metatarsal bases and presence of bony fragments.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Right foot pain due to a Lisfranc fracture (fracture to the second metatarsal bone and top of the foot).
- Order an MRI to assess for any injuries to the ligaments; MRI will be done this afternoon at the outpatient facility downstairs.
- Discussed that surgery is most likely needed to realign bones and ligaments using plates and screws to prevent loss of the arch, flat-footedness, and arthritis. Surgery would be an outpatient procedure performed the next day, though the patient requested time to think about it.
- Post-procedure plan would include a cast, crutches, non-weight-bearing for 6-8 weeks, a 24-hour post-procedure follow-up, and a 2-week follow-up.

Right-sided back pain and blood in urine, diagnosed with a kidney stone by PCP.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is an adult female presenting with right-sided back pain for about a week. The pain has moved down slightly to her right lower side and is described as pretty constant. She also noticed blood in her urine, though she denies any pain with urination. She tried taking ibuprofen, which helped a little bit, but it still hurts. She reports feeling a little bit nauseated, but denies throwing up, fever, or chills. This is her first time having a kidney stone, though her father has a history of kidney stones. She was evaluated by her PCP this morning and sent over due to concerns for a kidney stone. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Denies fever, chills.
Gastrointestinal: Reports feeling a little bit nauseated; denies vomiting.
Genitourinary: Reports blood in urine and right-sided flank/back pain; denies dysuria.
All other systems reviewed and negative except as noted in HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure and heart rate are fine; no fever.
Abdomen: Mild pain and tenderness to palpation of the abdomen. No rebound or guarding.
Flank: CVA located near flank tenderness on the right.

RESULTS
CT scan of the side showed a stone measuring 0.5 centimeters in size located in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right kidney stone (0.5 cm in the proximal right ureter).
2. Push fluids to facilitate passing the stone.
3. Prescribe ibuprofen 800 mg as needed for pain.
4. Provide a urine strainer to catch the stone when it passes.
5. Order a BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture; antibiotics may be prescribed based on urinalysis results if an infection is present.
6. Follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks. If still having symptoms, discuss further treatment such as lithotripsy.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right upper quadrant abdominal pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a patient referred by Dr. Miller for evaluation of right upper quadrant abdominal pain present for several weeks. The patient had an ultrasound ordered by Dr. Miller that revealed gallstones. The pain is described as a squeezing, severe pain located on the right side of the belly underneath the ribs. It comes and goes, rating up to an 8 out of 10 in severity, and is associated with nausea. The pain typically occurs immediately after eating or a couple of hours later. The patient has a history of type 2 diabetes, for which they cut back on sugar and started a keto diet, losing about 25 pounds over the last 3 months. High-fat foods in the keto diet (such as pork rinds) seemed to trigger the pain, and while cutting them back helped somewhat, the pain persists. The patient reports occasional low-grade fevers when the pain is severe for a couple of days, but denies vomiting. Family history is positive for gallbladder disease in both parents, who both had their gallbladders removed. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Positive for occasional low-grade fevers. Denies chills.
Gastrointestinal: Positive for right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and food-related symptom onset. Denies vomiting.
All other systems reviewed and negative except as noted above.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Blood pressure 128/88, respiratory rate 16, pulse rate 68, afebrile, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm; no ectopic beats, clicks, rubs, or murmurs.
Lungs: Clear and equal bilaterally to auscultation.
Abdomen: Positive bowel sounds, soft, non-distended. Positive for slight guarding to the right upper quadrant. No rebound tenderness. Positive Murphy's sign (patient exhibited guarding and reported severe pain with palpation beneath the right ribs upon inspiration). No peritoneal signs.

RESULTS
Abdominal Ultrasound: Shows multiple gallstones present in the gallbladder with mild thickening. Common bile duct size is within normal limits at 4.1 millimeters.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Mild cholecystitis with gallstones. No frank obstruction, but the gallbladder is inflamed.
2. Recommendation for surgical removal of the gallbladder via laparoscopic cholecystectomy (duration approximately 1 to 1.5 hours, with an overnight stay in the hospital for post-procedure monitoring).
3. Post-procedure instructions: Avoid high-frequency/high-fat foods, eat high-fiber foods. Take it easy for the first 24 hours; light walking on solid ground allowed within a day or two. Follow-up visit in about a week to clear the patient for return to normal activities.
4. Continue to monitor type 2 diabetes with primary care provider or endocrinologist, especially in light of upcoming surgery.

Left foot pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jean is a soccer player who presents with left foot pain after an injury during a soccer game yesterday. She was trying to steal the ball from another player who fell directly onto her right foot (noting later in the exam discussion that the injury is to the left foot), causing her body to twist and resulting in foot pain. She had to stop playing immediately and was helped off the field. She has been treating the pain with elevation, ice, a wrap applied by the trainer, and ibuprofen. Pain level is 3 with ibuprofen and 7-8 without ibuprofen. She denies any numbness, tingling, or strange sensations in the left foot. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 118/72, HR 58, RR 14, afebrile, O2 saturation 99% on room air.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no clicks, rubs, murmurs, or ectopic beats.
Respiratory: Lungs clear and equal bilaterally.
Focused Left Foot Exam: Bruising on the bottom and top of the foot, associated swelling, tenderness to palpation of the midfoot, and positive piano key test. 
Neurovascular: Brisk capillary refill of less than 3 seconds, dorsalis pedis pulse intact and strong, motor and sensation intact to light touch.

RESULTS
X-ray shows subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal with a 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and the presence of a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left foot pain due to a Lisfranc fracture (fracture to the second metatarsal bone with involvement of the Lisfranc joint space).
- Order an MRI to assess for ligament injury.
- Recommend surgery to place bones back in proper position using plates and screws. This is a outpatient day surgery.
- Patient will follow up in the clinic, be placed in a cast, use crutches, and remain non-weight-bearing on the left foot for approximately 6 to 8 weeks, followed by gradual return to walking.
- Discussed risks of non-treatment, including loss of the foot arch (becoming flat-footed) and high likelihood of developing arthritis.
- Patient will follow up on Monday morning.

She experiences occasional lightheadedness and dizziness, for which she takes a pill (meclizine) only when it gets bad, but denies any passing out or irregular heartbeats. She reports ankle swelling for about six months that fluctuates. She has experienced a gradual weight loss of about 10 pounds over the past year, currently weighing 120 pounds. She also reports feeling overly tired.

Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain, passing out, and irregular heartbeats. Reports shortness of breath with exertion/overexertion and ankle swelling.
Gastrointestinal: Not discussed.
Genitourinary: Not discussed.
Musculoskeletal: Reports severe leg pain in both legs for about a month.
Neurological: Reports lightheadedness and dizziness.

Hematuria and renal ultrasound results.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Kelly Wood is an established patient seen for a renal ultrasound because of hematuria. The patient reports that over the past six weeks, she has had a few episodes of bright red urine the color of cherry Kool-Aid. Last week, she was constantly having to pee and it hurt "something terrible," rating the pain at an 8 out of 10 at the time. She notes she passed what looked like two small stones last week after scheduling this appointment. After passing those stones, things have felt a lot better, and she is currently denying any flank pain or tenderness in her lower back. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: No flank pain. 
Genitourinary: Normal vaginal exam.

RESULTS
Urine dipstick today: Negative for leukocytes, nitrates, protein, ketone, bilirubin, and glucose. Color is yellow and clear, urobilinogen 0.2, pH 5.5, specific gravity 1.020. Trace amount of blood in the urine, intact.
Renal ultrasound impression: 
- Right kidney: 10 cm in length by 5 cm wide. No stones, masses, or hydronephrosis.
- Left kidney: 10.8 cm in length by 5 cm wide. There is a 6 mm left renal stone, non-obstructing.
- Pre-void volume: 533 mL.
- Post-void volume: 0 mL.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Hematuria, secondary to kidney stones. The blood in the urine is due to the kidney stones; fortunately, she passed two last week and the blood has nearly subsided.
2. Chronic urolithiasis. One non-obstructing 6 mm stone remains in the left kidney. Since it is not obstructing or causing pain, no surgical intervention is recommended at this time.
3. Lifestyle and dietary counseling provided to prevent future stone formation:
   - Increase water intake to about half of body weight in ounces per day (125 ounces of water daily for her weight of 250 pounds).
   - Avoid sugary drinks like Mountain Dew.
   - Avoid foods rich in sodium, oxalate, and animal protein. Consume less than 1,000 milligrams of sodium a day and reduce beef, poultry, fish, and pork. Avoid oxalate-rich foods such as spinach, chocolate, beets, rhubarb, and soy products.
   - Provided a handout reviewing dietary recommendations and foods to avoid.
4. Follow-up in one year, provided no further issues arise. Patient instructed to call the office sooner if she experiences issues like bleeding or pain, and to go to the emergency room if she experiences severe pain or bright red blood in her urine.

Not discussed.

Abnormal lab finding (low hemoglobin), fatigue, and dizziness.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 49-year-old female with a past medical history of congestive heart failure, kidney stones, and prior colonoscopy who presents for an abnormal lab finding. Over the past couple of months, she has experienced significant fatigue and dizziness, feeling worn out with normal activities like walking a mile or going to work. She denies blood in stools, dark or tarry stools, heavy menstrual bleeding, passing out, significant weight loss, or loss of appetite. She reports a history of mild diverticulosis found on a colonoscopy about three years ago with no issues since. Regarding her congestive heart failure, she admits to struggling more recently with salt intake due to traveling (e.g., eating McDonald's cheeseburgers in Vermont) and has noticed some swelling in her legs, but denies shortness of breath or orthopnea. Regarding kidney stones, she reports no recent flare-ups, back or flank pain, or blood in urine. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for fatigue, dizziness, trace-to-one-plus lower extremity swelling, and mild nasal congestion due to seasonal allergies. All other systems reviewed were negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs are fine, and blood pressure and heart rate are normal. 
Heart: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur (previously noted).
Lower extremities: Trace to 1+ pitting edema in the ankles.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram (from about 6 months ago): Shows low pumping function (ejection fraction at about 45%) and moderate mitral regurgitation.
Hemoglobin: Low at 8.2.

1. Anemia (low hemoglobin of 8.2): Send off an anemia profile and more labs to determine the type of anemia. Refer the patient to gastroenterology for evaluation, likely for an endoscopy and another colonoscopy.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female who presents with right foot pain after an injury playing tennis a couple of days ago. She was trying to volley the ball, got in front of another player, and fell on top of her foot. She twisted around to catch herself and felt pain. She was unable to continue playing and had to be held from the field because she could not put weight on her foot. Since the injury, she wrapped it with an ace wrap from the clubhouse, iced it last night, kept it elevated on a pillow, and took ibuprofen, which helps a little bit before wearing off. She reports no numbness or tingling and states she can still feel her foot. She has no prior history of injury to this foot, though she previously injured her left leg.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Not discussed.
Eyes: Not discussed.
Ent: Not discussed.
Respiratory: Stridor appreciated; no wheezes or rales.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmur, rub, or gallop.
Gastrointestinal: No rebound, no guarding.
Genitourinary: Not discussed.
Musculoskeletal: Right foot pain, inability to bear weight.
Skin: Head is symmetrical, mucosal membranes normal, not hot to touch. Right foot bruising, swelling, and warmth to touch.
Neurological: No numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation.
Psychiatric: Not discussed.
Endocrine: Not discussed.
Hematologic/Immunologic: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 125/70, respiratory rate 18, temperature 97.1 F, SpO2 100%, pulse 60 bpm.
General: Vitals look great.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur, rub, or gallop.
Lungs: Stridor appreciated, no wheezes or rales.
Abdomen: No rebound, no guarding.
Head and Neck: Symmetrical, mucosal membranes normal, not hot to touch.
Right Foot Exam: Bruising of the plantar and dorsal aspects, associated swelling, tenderness to palpation of the midfoot, positive piano key test of the first and second metatarsals, warm to touch. Neurovascularly: capillary refill less than 3 seconds, strong dorsalis pedis pulse, and sensation intact to light touch.
Left Foot Exam: Normal, capillary refill appropriate, pedal pulses strong, sensation intact.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot: Subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal with a 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and the presence of a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right foot pain consistent with a Lisfranc fracture.
2. Recommended surgery to place the bones in proper positions using plates and screws to prevent complications such as poor bone alignment, poor ligament healing, loss of the arch (flat-footedness), and arthritis. The procedure is a day surgery (patient goes home the same day).
3. MRI ordered to further assess the fracture and ligament injury.
4. Post-procedure care: Follow up in clinic in about a week, cast, crutches, and non-weight-bearing status for 6-8 weeks, followed by gradual walking based on progress. Physical therapy recommended after surgery.
5. Patient will need someone else to drive her home; she is out for the rest of the tennis season.
6. Surgical risks (bleeding, loss of sensation, nerve damage) to be reviewed with paperwork by the medical assistant.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after inferior STEMI and new stent placement.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female with a history of coronary artery disease (status post RCA stent in 2018), hypertension, and diabetes, who presents for follow-up after a recent inferior STEMI requiring another stent. She reports that the event was a shock, as she thought she was doing fine, but she experienced horrible, persistent chest pain similar to her first heart attack, prompting an emergency room visit where the new stent was placed. She currently denies ongoing chest pain or shortness of breath. She is able to walk her dog 1.5 to 2 miles daily. She notes some mild leg swelling since discharge from the hospital. She can lie flat at night, though she uses a couple of pillows. She is able to afford her medications and is taking them as prescribed. Regarding her diet, she admits she has been less strict about salt intake recently, noting a fondness for pizza with pepperoni and fries, but agrees to work on reducing her salt intake. She manages her diabetes and blood sugars with metformin to avoid insulin.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for acute chest pain or shortness of breath currently. Positive for mild lower extremity swelling since hospital discharge. No significant orthopnea (uses a couple of pillows, sleeps mostly normal). 

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Look good.
Neck: No jugular venous distention, no carotid bruits.
Heart: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base.
Lungs: Clear.
Extremities: Lower limb edema present, pitting 1+ on the right. Right radial artery cath site is clean, dry, and intact without hematoma. Right radial artery pulses are palpable.

RESULTS
EKG: Normal sinus rhythm, good R-wave progression, and evolutionary changes anticipated after a STEMI.
Echocardiogram: Reduced ejection fraction of 35% and moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Coronary Artery Disease: Continue aspirin 81 mg daily, Brilinta 90 mg twice daily, Lipitor 80 mg daily, and Toprol 50 mg daily. Referral to cardiac rehab.
2. Newly reduced left ventricular dysfunction and moderate mitral regurgitation: Likely stunned myocardium expected to improve over time. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily. Repeat echocardiogram in about 2 months.
3. Acute heart failure (fluid retention): Prescribe Lasix 40 mg once daily and add Aldactone 12.5 mg daily. Obtain lab work.
4. Hypertension and Diabetes: Continue metformin. Blood pressure is fine; will use Aldactone. Nutrition counseling recommended to address diet, particularly sodium reduction and limiting preserved meats like pepperoni.

- Age at menarche: 13
- Age at menopause: 28
- Oral hormone replacement therapy: None
- History of endometriosis: None

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female who presents with right ankle pain after slipping and falling on ice yesterday while taking out the trash. She reports hearing a "pop" when she fell. Initially, she was unable to walk on it at all and was helped inside by a visiting friend. Today, she is able to put a little more weight on it, though she is still limping. She iced it last night, kept it elevated, and took ibuprofen last night and this morning. Her pain is currently a 6 out of 10 without ibuprofen, which decreases to a 1 out of 10 with ibuprofen. She denies any numbness or tingling in the right foot. She has no prior history of injury to this specific ankle, though she has a history of playing soccer in college and intramural soccer.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for numbness or tingling in the right foot. (All other systems not discussed).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Look good and everything looks okay.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right ankle showed no fracture.

- Keep the leg elevated when seated and continue to ice.
- Provide an aircast to help stabilize the ankle.
- Prescribe crutches; stay off the leg for now, then start walking on it as tolerated in a couple of days.
- Continue to take NSAIDs or ibuprofen as needed for pain and to reduce inflammation and swelling.
- Symptoms should significantly improve over a few weeks.
- Follow-up in 14 days.

The patient is a with type 2 diabetes who presents with a nonhealing right foot ulcer present for about a year. The patient reports no pain due to lack of feeling in the foot (neuropathy), but notes an increase in drainage lately and feeling a little more tired. The patient denies fever or chills. Blood sugars have been running in the 200s, and the last A1c was about 10. Medications include metformin and insulin. The patient plans to walk around at the zoo over the weekend wearing regular shoes.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Feels a little more tired. Denies fever, chills.
Cardiovascular: Not discussed.
Respiratory: Not discussed.
Gastrointestinal: Not discussed.
Genitourinary: Not discussed.
Musculoskeletal: Not discussed.
Neurological: Decreased feeling in the foot (neuropathy). No pain at the wound site.
Dermatological: 1 x 2 cm circular wound on the right foot with increased drainage.
Endocrinologist/Other: Type 2 diabetes with blood sugars in the 200s and A1c around 10.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Vitals look good; no fever.
Right Foot Exam: 1 x 2 centimeter circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the fifth MTP joint. Yellow slough present with minimal granulation tissue. She feels her bowel regimen includes Miralax regularly and lactulose as a rescue medication. She notes the hot and humid weather during late June may have contributed to dehydration and worsening constipation.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
New right eye twitch.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Karen Nelson is a 3-year-old female with no significant past medical history who presents with a new right eye twitch noticed by her father a couple of weeks ago. The father reports seeing the twitch several times an hour on some days, while other days it is not seen until the late afternoon, occurring every day for the last several weeks. When the twitch occurs, the whole side of her face moves for several seconds, and she is left blinking frequently. Karen feels her face sometimes and reports an urge to move her face followed by feeling better. The twitch does not hurt. Karen continues playing or doing whatever she was doing when it happens. She has been eating well, playing with friends, and going about normal activities. Father brought a video of the twitch. There is no history of seizures. No family history of seizures or Tourette syndrome.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for fever, chills, coughing, headache, and sleep problems. 

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurological exam: Patient is awake, alert, and oriented times three. Speech is clear and fluent. Cranial nerves are intact without focal neurologic findings. Gait is steady, heel-toe walking is normal. No pronator drift. Sensation is intact. Reflexes are 2+ and symmetric at the biceps, triceps, knees, and ankles.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Eye tics (transient tics). The doctor suspects tics rather than seizures, noting the same part of the body moves each time and the patient reports an urge followed by relief. 
Plan: The best approach is to ignore the tics so as not to draw attention to them, which can make them worse. Tics are common in children and often disappear within a year. No treatment (pills or creams) is recommended at this time since she is doing well overall and it has not impacted her activities, but treatment can be considered if it worsens.

Follow-up visit, acne, weight gain, and medication costs.

She was also charged $100 for a gel medication. She inquires about weight gain and if it could be related to her previous birth control or polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). She has tried to improve her diet and plans to return to the gym in July after her contract hold and vacation. She asks about supplements like CLA, chromium, and amino acids for weight loss/metabolism. She notes sensitive skin, foot swelling, and constipation. She is interested in learning about the weight loss study but decides to wait for a little bit. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for sensitive skin, foot swelling, and constipation. 
All other systems reviewed are negative unless otherwise noted in the HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Lungs: Clear to auscultation.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm.
Extremities: Feet and ankles examined; no acute edema noted at the time of the exam.

RESULTS
- Dexamethasone suppression test: Passed/normal (rules out Cushing's syndrome).
- Salivary cortisol: Two completely normal, one abnormal; may need repeat in the future.
- Total cholesterol: 222 (High)
- HDL (Good cholesterol): 44 (Low, should be >50)
- LDL (Bad cholesterol): 153 (High, should be <100)

- Vitamin D: Vitamin D deficiency noted.

- Liver enzymes: ALT is 30 (significantly improved from 128 previously and 254 in October, dropping after stopping medication in December).

- Vitamin D deficiency: Continue vitamin D; start 2,000 IU daily after finishing current dose to maintain levels.
- Hyperlipidemia / Cholesterol: Advise low-carb diet, avoid alcohol, fatty foods, and low-cholesterol foods.
- Contraception: Discussed stopping birth control and alternative option Phexxi (spermicide gel) applied before intercourse.

Reports that bigger pieces of food feel like they are getting stuck, though it does not happen every time he eats. Diet has recently consisted of more pizza and burgers due to stress from an upcoming cross-country move from the west coast to the east coast and increased alcohol and caffeine intake. Denies weight loss; notes he has actually gained some weight. Reports occasional upper belly (epigastric) pain. Denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, blood in stool, or dark tarry stools.

General: Gained about 10 pounds over the last month. Denies weight loss.
Gastrointestinal: Reports difficulty swallowing, pain with swallowing in the chest, and occasional upper abdominal pain. Denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, blood in stool, or dark tarry stools.

Vitals: Blood pressure 133/70, heart rate good, afebrile, O2 saturation 100%, respiratory rate 19.
General: No rash, no lesion, no bruising.
Eyes: Pupils equal and reactive to light.

- Recommend diet changes: decrease alcohol and caffeine, avoid citrus fruits and spicy foods, eat slowly, and chew food more thoroughly.
- Follow-up visit scheduled for next week for the endoscopy.

Not discussed.

Hospital follow-up after anterior STEMI.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Russell Ramirez is a 45-year-old male with a past medical history significant for CAD status post prior RCA stent in 2018, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus, who presents for hospital follow-up after an anterior STEMI, now status post drug-eluting stent to the LAD, newly reduced ejection fraction of 35%, and moderate mitral regurgitation. He reports feeling pretty good overall, though he feels tired every now and then. He denies chest pain or shortness of breath. He has been doing short walks around the block and light housekeeping. He sleeps with two pillows, which is normal for him, and denies orthopnea. He denies leg swelling and notes he has always had skinny ankles. He is able to afford his medications and is taking them as prescribed. He is trying to watch his salt intake and change his diet, acknowledging he needs to cut back on salty foods like pizza.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for occasional fatigue. Negative for fever or chills.
Cardiovascular: Negative for chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and lower extremity edema.
Respiratory: Negative for shortness of breath or cough.
All other systems reviewed and were negative unless otherwise noted.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Look good.
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Heart: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base, stable compared to last year.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Extremities: No swelling or edema. Right radial artery cath site is clean, dry, and intact without hematoma. Palpable radial pulse.

RESULTS
EKG showed normal sinus rhythm, good R wave progression, and evolutionary changes which are anticipated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Coronary artery disease: Continue aspirin 81 mg daily, Brilinta 90 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg daily, and Toprol 50 mg daily. Referred to cardiac rehab for education and exercise confidence.
2. Newly reduced left ventricular dysfunction and moderate mitral regurgitation: Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily. Add aldactone 12.5 mg daily. No diuretic needed at this time. Obtain labs next week. Repeat echocardiogram in about 2 months.
3. Hypertension: Blood pressures are fine at this time; continue to monitor. Patient will likely tolerate aldactone well.

Right shoulder injury.

He reports no numbness or tingling in the fingers, and grip strength is okay for tasks like grabbing a cup of coffee. He notes a slight headache from hitting his head slightly when he fell, but denies passing out, fever, chills, or neck problems. Other joints on the right arm (elbow, wrist) are unaffected. Constitutional: No fever or chills; reports a slight headache. 
Neurological: No numbness or tingling in the fingers; no loss of consciousness.
Neck: No neck pain or stiffness.
Musculoskeletal: Right shoulder pain; no other joint pain.
All other systems not discussed.

Vitals: Blood pressure 122/76, heart rate 82 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, afebrile.

She denies chest pain or tightness, fevers, or chills, but notes bringing up "yuck" occasionally in the morning. She has not been regularly checking her blood sugars with an accu-check; her last reading a couple of weeks ago was around 230. She reports urinating frequently despite not drinking very much. She endorses lower back pain that limits her activity, with no weakness or numbness in her legs.

Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or tightness. Reports lower extremity swelling and rapid weight gain.
Respiratory: Reports orthopnea (choking sensation when lying down), intermittent shortness of breath at night, and occasional morning phlegm. Denies daytime exertional shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.
Genitourinary: Reports frequent urination.
Musculoskeletal: Reports chronic lower back pain. Denies leg weakness or numbness.
Endocrine: Blood sugars running high (home reading around 230).

Neck: JVD present, no bruits.

Not discussed.

- Increase Lasix dose from 20 mg to 60 mg daily for the next four days.
- Weigh daily.
- Use albuterol and Atrovent inhalers (refill provided).

- Provide exercises to help get off the couch and improve blood sugar.
- Consider physical therapy if pain and medication do not resolve symptoms.

Ongoing management of rheumatoid arthritis and right knee pain/swelling.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Tyler Nelson is a 74-year-old male here for ongoing management of rheumatoid arthritis. Last visit he received a steroid injection in his right knee, which helped for about a couple of weeks. He reports his knee is still swollen and pretty painful, and now the whole right leg is getting swollen. The whole leg swelling started about two months ago (a couple of weeks after his last visit). Pain level is currently about a 3, but typically around a 6 on a normal day. Compression socks help to some degree, but the leg is still swollen, especially around the knee. He reports stiffness when getting up after sitting, requiring a cane to get his bearings until it loosens up. Medications include Xeljanz XR 11 mg daily and Celebrex 200 mg daily (started about 2 months ago).

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Range of motion slightly diminished in the right knee; patient states it hurts when he tries to straighten it all the way. Pitting edema noted around the knee and ankle. Normal capillary refill in the toes. The area is sore like an old bruise. The right knee feels hot to touch, indicating inflammation.

RESULTS
CMP levels are good (noted that Xeljanz is a high-risk medication requiring CMP levels checked every couple of months).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Rheumatoid arthritis with right knee pain, inflammation, and whole leg edema/swelling.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Rachel is a 48-year-old female with a history of depression, smoking, and chronic back pain, presenting with shortness of breath. She reports palpitations and shortness of breath during very mild exercises or walking, such as walking up her driveway. She notes this happens more often lately. She has been exercising more recently to try to get rid of the "covid 15." She has cut down on her smoking significantly, down to about once a day from two packs a day previously. 

Regarding her depression, she has her moments with some days feeling extremely low. She continues to take Effexor, and her depression is considered stable. For her chronic back pain, she continues to take gabapentin (Neurontin), which is helping control the pain, though it does come back every now and then, for which she tries to get rest. She has not made yoga a habit.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Physical exam is pretty normal other than mild wheezes in all lung fields.

RESULTS
Pulmonary function tests suggest possible asthma or COPD.
Chest X-ray shows a slightly flatter diaphragm, which can be seen in COPD and happens with smokers often.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease): Diagnosed based on pulmonary function tests, X-ray, and exam showing mild wheezes. 
   - Prescribed Combivent inhaler, two puffs twice a day to help open up lungs.
   - Prescribed Albuterol inhaler, two puffs as needed as a rescue medication for when she gets really short of breath.
   - Prescribed a Prednisone taper pack.
2. Depression: Stable. Continue taking Effexor. Encourage yoga for depression and back pain.
3. Chronic back pain: Continue taking Neurontin (gabapentin).

Right elbow pain.

   - Order an A1c test.
   - Referral to diabetic counseling/dietitian.
   - Follow up in a couple of weeks.

   - Continue lisinopril at 10 mg daily.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right index finger pain and stiffness following a motor vehicle accident.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip Gutierrez is a 50-year-old male presenting for a second opinion regarding his right index finger. He sustained a hyperextension injury to the right index finger during a motor vehicle accident in March (approximately three months ago) when he was rear-ended and felt his finger stretch out as he was slung forward. He reports continued swelling, inability to make a fist, and pain that is sometimes unbearable, even making driving difficult. He previously saw an orthopedist and an occupational therapist, and was sent for an MRI. He reports being told he has a tear in his finger, but received conflicting information regarding injections and surgery from previous providers. He works as an x-ray tech and is right-handed.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Takes a blood pressure medication. History of itching/reaction to methylprednisolone and dexamethasone (causes his heart to race). Otherwise, review of systems is negative except as noted in the history of present illness.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant, cooperative, healthy male in no distress.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, 2+ radial pulse.
Right Hand / Index Finger: No swelling or bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases, slightly diminished over the PIP of the index finger compared to the middle finger. Index finger rests in a 10-degree PIP-flexed position. Attempting to correct the position is uncomfortable. Pushing on the finger causes pain and numbness. Attempting to bend the tip elicits a feeling of tearing. Bending at the MCP joint causes pain and stretching discomfort. Extensor tendons and collateral ligaments are intact.

RESULTS
MRI of the right index finger (4/24/2021): Showed focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint, partial-thickness tear of the right FDS (flexor digitorum superficialis), and fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint were intact, as was the MCP joint capsule. Extensor tendons deemed intact.
X-rays (four views of the right hand today): No bony abnormalities, joint congruency throughout all lesser digits on the right hand, no soft tissue shadows of concern, no arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Post-traumatic severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger with a partial tear of the FDS tendon.
2. Attempted steroid injection: Attempted to inject 1 cc of Celestone (betamethasone) with 0.5 cc of lidocaine into the flexor tendon sheath. The first attempt was aborted due to a dramatic and painful reaction by the patient withdrawing the hand. A second attempt was successfully performed using 1 cc of Celestone and 0.5 cc of lidocaine. A small palmar vein bled a scant amount, which was cleaned and a band-aid applied.
3. Post-procedure care: Reassured patient, recommended icing this evening and taking ibuprofen. Driving is permitted.
4. Physical/Occupational Therapy: Outpatient therapy once a week for six weeks with the goal of full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions. Patient needs to work on active bending and mobility.

Left knee pain.

Not discussed.

A subsequent CT scan confirmed the nodule. He is a former smoker who quit about 7 years ago. He denies any current pain or shortness of breath.

Constitutional: Denies fever.
Respiratory: Denies cough (resolved), denies shortness of breath.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain.

Extremities: Skin is pink, warm, and dry. No lower extremity edema. Mild swelling noted to knuckles on the third digit of each hand consistent with RA. Pulses intact in all extremities, capillary refill brisk.

   - Continue current management with methotrexate (7.5 mg weekly) and follow up with rheumatologist.

Numbness and tingling in both hands.

The patient was in a car wreck last December where he broke both wrists and hit his head (sustaining a contusion); he noticed the symptoms more once the wrists healed. His right wrist was in worse shape from the accident. He wears a splint on his right wrist and sometimes on the left, which helps. He also reports mild stiffness in his neck. Symptoms include soreness, occasional throbbing, and weakness when using the hands. Tingling happens more when they hurt, and is dull when it goes away. Symptoms occur more at night and come and go throughout the day. He reports no complete loss of sensation, though hands may be less sensitive. He was prescribed nerve pain medicine but has not been taking it as directed. Past medical history includes hypertension (taking Coreg), anxiety (taking Lexapro), and prediabetes (controlled by diet). No history of thyroid issues.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fatigue and weight gain.
Eyes: Floaters.
Cardiovascular: Shortness of breath and leg swelling.
Gastrointestinal: Excessive appetite and bloating.
Endocrine: Always hungry.
Skin: Nail bed changes, dryness, and itching.
Musculoskeletal: Gout and muscle pain.
The remainder of the review of systems is negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurologic examination:
Right hand: Sensation is normal, except pinprick sensation is diminished in the third and fourth fingers.

Not discussed.

- Follow-up visit after tests are complete.
- Continue wearing splints.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Adult hydrocephalus follow-up after shunt surgery.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Watson is an 86-year-old male presenting in follow-up for adult hydrocephalus, three months after undergoing shunt surgery on August 1st, 2020. He has a history of progressive gait impairment, cognitive impairment, and decreased bladder control for 8 to 10 years prior to surgery. A Medtronic strata programmable shunt in the ventricular peritoneal configuration was placed and programmed at a level 2.0. Since surgery, he has not been hospitalized. His walking has improved; he is able to walk to the dining room just fine, though he still requires assistance at times. Bladder control improved some after surgery but has leveled out, and he continues to wear diapers without sores, decreased urination, or painful urination. Cognition has improved; he reports not feeling lost when talking to someone anymore, and his daughter and sister note he can have a normal conversation again. He denies headaches, pain where the shunt is, or belly pain. Regarding driving, the doctor notes it is unlikely his movement speed will improve enough to pass a driver safety evaluation currently, but it could potentially improve over a 9 to 12 month range.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Significant for impaired ability to carry out daily functions. Negative for fever or unintentional weight loss.
GU: Significant for urinary incontinence and wearing a diaper. Negative for genital sores, decreased or painful output.
Neurological: Significant for continued walking impairment and cognitive impairment. Negative for headaches, recent falls, or hallucinations.
Psychiatric: Negative for depression, excessive worrying, or mood swings.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 124/80, heart rate 64, respirations 18, weight 174 pounds, pain 0/10.
General: Pleasant and cooperative man, able to converse easily with additional details provided by his daughter.
Shunt site: Clean, dry, and intact with a confirmed setting of 2.
Cognitive testing: MMSE score of 26 out of 30 when tested with spelling and 25 out of 30 when tested with calculations (slight improvement from initial scores of 23 and 24). Able to get 2 of 3 memory words with cuing and the third with multiple choice.
Gait testing: Tinetti assessment tool without an assistive device showed a gait score of 6-8 out of 12 and balance score of 12 out of 16 for a total score of 18-20 out of 28 (slightly improved from initial score of 15-17 out of 28).
Cranial Nerves: Pupils equal, EOMs intact, face symmetric, no dysarthria.
Motor: Normal for bulk and strength.
Coordination: Slow from finger-to-nose.

RESULTS
Head CT scan from 10/15/2020: Shows a frontal horn span at the level of foramen of Monro of 4.6 centimeters with a third ventricular contour that is flat with a span of 10 millimeters. There is a tiny amount of blood in the right frontal region with a tiny subdermal collection (not noted by the radiologist). There is also substantial small vessel ischemic change.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Adult hydrocephalus
- Gait impairment
- Urinary incontinence and urgency
- Cognitive impairment

Plan: Leave the shunt set at level 2.0 for another 2 to 3 months before considering changes, given the patient's overall improvement and lack of headaches or pain despite the tiny blood fluid collection on CT. Return in 3 months for follow-up. The patient may enroll in a driver safety program preemptively if desired, though formal recommendation is deferred until further potential improvement over the next 9 to 12 months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
High blood pressure and palpitations.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 49-year-old male with a history of hypertension starting at a young age and palpitations. He was recently seen in the emergency room in March with high blood pressure and palpitations, which he attributes to having a few cups of coffee without breakfast, suspecting it was a panic attack rather than a cardiac event. He has not experienced palpitations since. He reports issues with his blood pressure since he was young and notes a family history of high blood pressure. He was put on a new combination medication about a month ago by a new primary care doctor. He takes Benicar HCT (hydrochlorothiazide 40-25) and amlodipine 10 mg daily. He checks his blood pressure every morning and reports recent readings running around 146 to 155. He is trying to back off on his salt intake and tries to walk on the treadmill when he can. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Heart and lungs sound good. Abdomen is soft, non-tender to palpation. Extremities show no ankle or foot swelling. 

RESULTS
Potassium level one week ago was 4.0.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Resistant hypertension, currently on multiple maximum dose medications without adequate control.
- Add spironolactone to the medication regimen to target potential hormonal/aldosterone-driven hypertension.
- Discussed risks of hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone, including electrolyte balance, dehydration, potential increase in potassium, and decrease in sodium. 
- Discussed rare side effects of spironolactone including dizziness and gynecomastia (chest tenderness, swollen or enlarged breasts); instructed to stop the medication and notify the clinic if gynecomastia occurs.
- Order a metabolic panel (blood tests) and schedule a follow-up visit in two weeks to check blood pressure and electrolytes.
- Provided education on the DASH eating plan (heart.org) and lifestyle modifications: keeping sodium under 2000 mg/day (ideally 1500 mg/day), increasing potassium, and performing routine treadmill exercise for 30 minutes most days.
- Future plan: If spironolactone is ineffective, refer the patient to the resistant hypertension clinic to evaluate for secondary causes and potential procedures such as renal denervation.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
High blood pressure.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Virginia is a female who presents for evaluation of uncontrolled hypertension, referred by her new primary care physician (PCP) after noting high blood pressure and concerns regarding her kidneys on recent blood work. The patient reports she feels fine most days and is busy at work, but she can tell when her blood pressure is high. She checks her blood pressure a few times a week using an electronic arm blood pressure cuff at home, and recently noticed readings as high as 170/90. Her PCP has made multiple medication adjustments, and she is currently taking Norvasc 10 mg daily and carvedilol 25 mg twice a day (previously on lisinopril). She admits to occasional use of NSAIDs (advil, motrin, aleve) for knee and back pain. Diet-wise, she admits to eating pizza, wings, and subs frequently during football season, though she tries to cut down on non-game days. Alcohol intake consists of a couple of beers during the week and 1-2 on the weekends. Family history is positive for high blood pressure in both parents and kidney disease in one parent.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Most days feels fine. 
Headaches: Mild headaches only when blood pressure gets very high; no regular headaches.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain. No shortness of breath, even with exertion. Mild lower extremity swelling if on her feet for a long time.
All other systems reviewed and negative except as noted.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 169/74, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 98%.
Neck: No jugular vein distention, no carotid bruits.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation.
Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur with an extra sound heard.
Extremities: 1+ pitting edema bilaterally.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Uncontrolled hypertension, likely multifactorial.
Plan:
1. Order renal artery ultrasound to rule out narrowing in blood vessels of the kidneys.
2. Order morning aldosterone levels, renin levels, and a 24-hour urine collection to evaluate adrenal glands.
3. Decrease alcohol intake to 1 to 2 drinks a week.
4. Be very judicious about decreasing salt intake.
5. Referral to a nutritionist to discuss dietary changes and salt reduction.
6. Stop taking NSAIDs (Advil, Motrin, Aleve); use Tylenol for pain instead.
7. Prescribe Cardura 4 mg once daily.
8. Keep a written record of home blood pressures taken at the same time every day for the next three weeks.
9. Return to the office in three weeks with blood pressure records.

He reports that when he stands up real fast, he gets really dizzy. He takes Tylenol for headaches and has thrown out Motrin and Advil due to his kidney disease.
